Observation of weakly damped modes using high resolution measurement of turbulence in a dipole confined plasma

Published Online: 2 January 2020

## ABSTRACT

When plasma is conﬁned by a levitated superconducting current ring, the turbulent radial particle ﬂux changes the direction depending upon the gradient of the particle number within tubes of equal magnetic ﬂux [Garnier et al., Phys. Plasmas 24, 012506 (2017)]. When the density proﬁle is highly peaked, the particle ﬂux is outward. When the density proﬁle is less peaked, turbulence drives an inward “particle pinch.” This change in the direction of particle ﬂux coincides with a reversal of the mean toroidal propagation direction of turbulent ﬂuctuations. Previously, only the mean wavenumber of the ﬂuctuations was reported. The mean wavenumber was computed from the ensemble correlation between two probes. Here, the full frequency-wavenumber power spectrum of the saturated turbulence is calculated by applying Capon’s “maximum likelihood method” to ﬂoating potential measurements from an array of probes. The power spectrum shows that the highest intensity modes are due to unstable entropy modes, and the less intense modes coincide with weakly damped convective cells, which rotate toroidally in the direction opposite to the unstable modes. Because the weakly damped modes make up a signiﬁcant fraction of the ﬂuctuating power, these measurements imply that saturated turbulence in a dipole-conﬁned plasma involves the excitation of weakly damped rotating convective cells.

A levitated superconducting current ring provides a simple toroidal magnetic conﬁguration for the study of plasma conﬁnement and turbulent radial transport.1 The magnetic ﬁeld is axisymmetric and without shear; plasma can be sustained in the steady state; and the plasma pressure remains stable up to the pressure of the magnetic ﬁeld without ﬁeld-aligned plasma currents and without fast magnetohydrodynamic instabilities, provided the pressure proﬁle is not excessively peaked.2 Laboratory experiments with levitated superconducting current rings have demonstrated steady toroidal conﬁnement at high plasma pressure,3,4 explored energetic particle instabilities,5 and studied turbulent radial transport and the inward curvature particle pinch.6,7

The characteristics of both the turbulence and the resulting particle transport in a dipole-conﬁned plasma were reported by Garnier and coauthors.8 Statistical measurements of the electrostatic ﬂuctuations and the radial particle ﬂux were compared for two different methods of particle fueling. When the plasma was fueled by deuterium gas at the outer edge of the plasma (called a “warm core”), the plasma proﬁle was characterized by a large ratio of the temperature to density

gradient scale length g > 2=3, where g  d ln Te=d ln n. When the plasma was fueled internally by injection of a lithium pellet (called a “cool core”), the central electron temperature cooled and the central density increased so that g < 2=3. In both cases, intermittent turbulent transport was driven by low frequency entropy modes dominated by long azimuthal wavelengths. However, the directions of both particle ﬂux and the mean toroidal phase velocity of the turbulence depended on whether g > 2=3 or g < 2=3. For edge gas fueling, g > 2=3, the particle transport was inward, and the mean phase velocity of the turbulence was in the electron magnetic drift direction. For internal pellet fueling, g < 2=3, the particle transport was outward, and the mean phase velocity of the turbulence was in the ion drift direction. The ﬂuctuations were identiﬁed as ﬂutelike entropy modes because the mean toroidal phase velocity of ﬂuctuations reversed direction as the mean particle ﬂux reversed, and this behavior is consistent with linear theory and quasilinear theory.9,10

Observations show that the ﬂuctuations are dominated by low toroidal mode numbers with chaotic phases and nonlinear spectral power transfer.12 Gyrokinetic simulations have shown the nonlinear excitation of Kelvin-Helmholtz instability, the generation of zonal ﬂow, and a sensitivity to plasma collisionality.13,14 However, these nonlinear effects have not been detected in experiments. Pioneeing studies of drift-wave instabilities by Cheng and Okuda,15 as well as by Weiland,16 show how the nonlinear excitations of stable convective cells lead to anomalous plasma transport. Recent gyrokinetic simulations by Fraser17 show nonlinear excitation of stable modes to be an essential feature of shear-ﬂow turbulence in magnetized plasma, provided dissipation is sufﬁciently low. Indeed, the nonlinear coupling of unstable eigenmodes to damped modes may make plasma turbulence fundamentally different from hydrodynamic turbulence.18

To better understand the characteristics of saturated turbulence in a dipole-conﬁned plasma, we extend the analysis reported in Ref. 8 using the ﬂoating probe data available online at the Zenodo repository.19 Plasma parameters, instrumentation, and discharge characteristics are described in Ref. 8. Here, we apply Capon’s “maximum likelihood method” (MLM)20,21 to the same ﬂoating potential measurements. We use all probe signals simultaneously and compute a distribution of wavenumbers for each frequency. This produces a 2D frequency-wavenumber power spectrum at higher resolution than that reported in Ref. 8. Consider a diagnostic array consisting of K probes located at toroidal angles /j. The sample rate is 125 kHz, so there are 87.5k time samples for each probe. This time interval was divided into a 220 ms period before pellet injection, a 30 ms period during pellet injection, and a 450 ms period after pellet injection. We ensemble average by partitioning the time before, during, and after into M nonoverlapping intervals: M ¼ 100 intervals (before), M ¼ 30 intervals (during), and M ¼ 125 intervals (after). Capon’s method has been applied to calculate the power spectra of space plasma turbulence,22 plasma waves measured by the CLUSTER23 and Magnetospheric Multiscale (MMS)24 spacecrafts, and scattering from ionospheric plasma.25 Capon’s MLM was selected for this analysis based on a determination that MLM produced the most accurate frequency-wavenumber power spectra among three digital methods. Besides (i) MLM, these analysis methods include (ii) a conventional two-dimensional short-time Fourier transform (STFT) method (e.g., similar to that described in Ref. 27) and (iii) a histogram method with the assumption that the turbulence is steady and homogeneous, described by Beall, Kim, and Powers.26 The symbols PC, PF, and PH are used to represent these three methods to compute the power spectrum. Validation data, consisting of three overlapping sine waves superimposed with Gaussian white-noise, were sampled in the same way as in the experiment. Noise levels from 5% to 50% were examined, and Capon’s method resulted in higher spectral power resolution in all cases. Two waves propagated in the electron drift direction with x=2p ¼ ð700; 500Þ Hz and n ¼ ð3; 1Þ, and one propagated in the ion drift direction with x=2p ¼ 200 Hz and n¼ –3. As compared with the STFT (PF), Capon’s MLM estimator (PC) ﬁlters modes to reduce variance while preserving the mean. MLM picks out the same peaks and ridges as the STFT but with signiﬁcantly less noise and reduced statistical variance on the signal. A third method (PH) uses histograms to estimate the frequencywavenumber power spectrum. As described by Beall, Kim, and Powers,26 a cross correlation is computed between ﬁxed probe pairs (as in Ref. 8), and the ensemble partition is treated as a statistical distribution to yield a 2D estimation. PH equates the mode numbers n proportionally to the cross phase of each partition.

Any of the three methods can be used to estimate the frequencywavenumber power spectrum, but Capon’s MLM reproduces the validation data most accurately. Figure 1 shows the power spectra computed by all three methods, PF, PC, and PH. Moreover, the MLM can uncover spectral features that are otherwise obscured since Capon’s MLM computes the most probable power spectrum. The MLM assumes that there exists a signal that propagates continuously across all probes, subject to Gaussian noise independently at each probe. A detailed derivation can be found in Capon’s monograph.21

*Figure 2 plots the frequency-wavenumber spectra before, during, and after pellet injection. This ﬁgure extends Fig. 5 of Ref. 8. Both before and after pellet injection, the dominant wave propagates in the electron magnetic drift direction. During pellet injection, the most intense ﬂuctuations reverse direction. The full frequency-wavenumber power spectra give insights into how electrostatic turbulence saturates in dipole-conﬁned plasma: the existence of modes propagating in the opposite direction of the unstable linear eigenmode. Figure 3 illustrates this feature of the power spectrum by showing PCðx; nÞ for x=2p ¼ 1 kHz and 2kHz for the time periods before lithium-pellet injection and after. In all cases, the mode number spectrum is broad with multiple modes propagating in both toroidal directions. For any given mode number n, the ﬂuctuations have a timevarying frequency with a broad frequency spectrum. This is consistent with previous observations.12 These features of the power spectrum were not indicated from the ensemble cross phase in Fig. 5 of Ref. 8. The processes leading to the saturated spectrum are not understood; however, the linear eigenmodes provide useful insights. The most intense modes correspond to unstable entropy modes. The modes with phase velocities in the opposite direction are weakly damped rotating convective cells. As described in Ref. 8, the linear gyroﬂuid equations deﬁne three modes: a pair of unstable and stable modes that copropagate in the same direction plus a weakly damped convective cell that propagates in the opposite direction. The three gyroﬂuid eigenmodes are given by Eqs. (4)–(6) of Ref. 8.
